title: Norman's 7 Principles for Making Hard Things Easy — Visual Exam Revision
description: Don Norman's seven principles of user-centered design, animated: knowledge in the world and in the head, simplify task structure, make things visible, get the mappings right, exploit constraints, design for error, and standardize.

scenes.title: Intro
lines: Ever pushed a door that said pull? That is not your fault. It is the designer's.
Don Norman's idea of user-centered design gives seven principles for making hard things easy.
Let's see each one, with a picture you can remember.

scenes.title: The 7 at a glance + mnemonic
lines: Here are the seven.
One, use knowledge in the world and in the head. Two, simplify task structure. Three, make things visible.
Four, get the mappings right. Five, exploit the power of constraints. Six, design for error. And seven, when all else fails, standardize.
First letters: K, S, V, M, C, E, S.
Kind Students Visit My College Every Saturday.

scenes.title: 1. Knowledge in the world and in the head
lines: Principle one. Use knowledge in the world, and knowledge in the head.
Knowledge in the world is on the screen: labels, menus, hints. New users do better when everything they need is in the interface.
Knowledge in the head is what you have memorized, like shortcuts. Experienced users are faster with it.
All users do better when the system's implementation model matches their mental model.
And avoid depending on user manuals. A manual is a very inconvenient part of the world.

scenes.title: 2. Simplify task structure
lines: Principle two. Simplify the task structure.
Consider the user's psychology: short term memory, long term memory, and concentration.
New technology should make tasks simpler, not harder.
Four ways. Keep the same task but add mental aids. Increase visibility. Automate the simple steps.
Or change the nature of the task entirely. Seven steps of booking become one tap.

scenes.title: 3. Make things visible
lines: Principle three. Make things visible.
Users should quickly see what they can do, how they can do it, and what will happen.
Possible actions should serve the user's goal. Norman calls this revenue, not excise. Real work, not overhead.
And system state should always be obvious.
Example: a course registration site should always show the current semester and the C R N you are working on.

scenes.title: 4. Get the mappings right
lines: Principle four. Get the mappings right.
Look at this stove. Four burners, four knobs in a row. Which knob controls which burner? You have to guess.
Now arrange the knobs in the same layout as the burners. The mapping is obvious.
Map intentions to actions, actions to effects, and system state to what is visible, and to what users need.
Graphics and icons are easier to understand. But designing good graphics is hard, and not a common skill among programmers.

scenes.title: 5. Exploit the power of constraints
lines: Principle five. Exploit the power of constraints.
Constraints stop users from entering wrong data in the first place.
Old stereo systems had dozens of wires, all alike. Modern ones use different connectors, so each plug only fits its own socket.
In software: date pickers on travel sites, radio buttons and dropdown lists, and ignoring dashes in phone and card numbers.
Think of it as strong typing for user interfaces.

scenes.title: 6. Design for error
lines: Principle six. Design for error.
Users are not perfect. They will enter invalid data. So design for invalid inputs.
Use constraints to avoid them. Correct them automatically when you can.
Make it simple to fix mistakes, and allow users to postpone corrections instead of blocking them.
And always, make it easy to undo.

scenes.title: 7. When all else fails, standardize
lines: Principle seven. When all else fails, standardize.
Think of car pedals. Accelerator on the right, brake to its left. In every car you rent.
Standard controls are all the same, so they only have to be learned once.
But it is a last resort, because it forces knowledge into the head.
And standardize early, or it will be too late.

scenes.title: Bonus: House of knowledge
lines: One bonus idea. Norman's book came out just before the web was proposed.
Berners-Lee built the web to make all information available to all users, all the time. Copying a file costs almost nothing, unlike writing a book.
So what was the biggest problem Norman expected? Finding what we want.

scenes.title: Recap
lines: Recap. Kind Students Visit My College Every Saturday.
Knowledge in world and head. Simplify tasks. Make things visible. Get the mappings right.
Exploit constraints. Design for error. And when all else fails, standardize.
Door, booking, stove, plugs, pedals. Remember the pictures, and you remember the principles.
